_metadata.independence: I read only u09-blind-input.json and consulted no other file, search, web page or API.

hints.reason: A bell rings (verb), while the moon side relies on the folk saying 'ring around the moon' (lunar halo); most players reach for Saturn first, so the moon side is only half-lit.
'Silver Bells' (the Christmas song) and the silver/silvery moon are both stock phrases, a defensible shared-property route like SWEET for APPLE+HONEY.

best_available.why: Both sides are familiar fixed phrases (Silver Bells, silvery moon) that a player will accept immediately.

pairs.pair_note: SILVER carries the pair; RING is a decent verb for BELL but the moon side depends on a weather saying.

hints.reason: Mouse eats cheese, but nothing recognizable ties cheese to a bell (a glass cheese bell/dome is far too niche), so this is one-sided filler.
Cat and mouse is the classic pairing, and a cat wears a collar bell / Aesop's mice 'bell the cat', one shared scene reaching both words.

best_available.why: The belled cat stalking a mouse is a single familiar scene that names both targets.

pairs.pair_note: CAT is excellent; CHEESE never touches BELL.

hints.reason: Christmas bells/Jingle Bells on one side; 'the night before Christmas', Christmas night and the carol Silent Night on the other, a shared festive scene.
Midnight bells (New Year, church chimes) would be a fine route, but MIDNIGHT literally contains the target NIGHT, which is a rule failure.

best_available.why: Christmas bells and Christmas night/Silent Night both read quickly and legally.

pairs.pair_note: MIDNIGHT fails only on the contains-target rule; CHRISTMAS is the serviceable hint.

hints.reason: Diving bell is a well-known compound and ocean diving is the obvious scene, so one word reaches both squarely.
A buoy floats in the ocean and a bell buoy is a real nautical compound; the bell side is moderately known rather than universal.

best_available.why: Diving bell plus ocean diving is a clean compound route on both sides.

pairs.pair_note: Two passes; DIVING is clearly stronger, BUOY leans on the bell-buoy compound.

hints.reason: Ship's bell is a familiar compound and pirate ship is the stock phrase, giving one nautical scene for both.

best_available.why: Ship's bell and pirate ship are both instant.

pairs.pair_note: Single strong hint.

hints.reason: Queen bee is strong, but there is no recognizable bee-to-bell link, so the hint is one-sided.
A queen's coronation is direct, and church bells pealing for a coronation is a familiar shared scene, if a secondary feature of it.

best_available.why: Royal ceremony with bells ringing out is a recognizable scene that contains both words.

pairs.pair_note: CORONATION is a fair scene hint; BEE does nothing for BELL.

hints.reason: Bells are cast metal (bell metal is even an alloy name) and robots are archetypally metal, a defensible shared-material route.

best_available.why: Both targets are strongly and immediately 'made of metal'.

pairs.pair_note: Material route only, but both sides are vivid enough to pass.

hints.reason: Bells are metal, and rock pairs with metal as music genres (rock and heavy metal) as well as mineral matter, so the rock side is more than a material match.

best_available.why: Bell metal plus rock/metal music gives two independent but familiar routes.

pairs.pair_note: Solid single hint.

hints.reason: Rose thorn is direct, but thorn has no recognizable link to a bell, so this is one-sided.
Belle and the enchanted rose (Beauty and the Beast) is a fine rose route, but BELLE contains and is essentially a spelling variant of the target BELL, a rule failure.

best_available.why: If the contains-target rule were waived, Belle's rose is a genuine story link; THORN never reaches BELL at all.

pairs.pair_note: No legal pass; BELLE fails on the rule, THORN on one-sidedness.

hints.reason: Bell pepper and salt and pepper are both everyday compounds, an excellent two-sided hint.

best_available.why: Compound on both sides with no stretch.

best_available.why: Only hint offered; the bell-tower half is strong and the shadow half is plausible if not specific.

pairs.pair_note: No pass; TOWER is the only candidate and the shadow link is loose.

hints.reason: Diving bell is the compound and shark (cage) diving is a familiar scene, so both sides are reached directly.

best_available.why: Compound plus well-known activity.

best_available.why: Only hint offered; the snake side is excellent and the bell side is reachable via a bell rattle toy.

pairs.pair_note: No pass; RATTLE is a near miss on the bell side.

pairs.pair_note: Strong single hint.

best_available.why: Compound plus the most ordinary water activity.

pairs.pair_note: Two passes; DIVING is the clearer serve.

hints.reason: Witch's broom is direct, but nothing links a broom to a bell, so this is one-sided filler.

Witches and candles are a familiar ritual image, and 'bell, book and candle' (the witchcraft/exorcism phrase and film) ties bell to candle, but that phrase is not widely known enough to call the bell side clear.

best_available.why: The bell-book-and-candle phrase genuinely binds all three ideas, so a knowing player gets both; BROOM reaches only the witch.

pairs.pair_note: No pass; CANDLE is a legitimate but niche route worth a second opinion.

hints.reason: Sheep wear bells (the bellwether), and wolf-and-sheep is a stock pairing, so a belled flock stalked by a wolf is one shared scene.

Bridge is a game and card game is a stock compound; broad but it reaches both words directly.

best_available.why: More specific than GAME while still immediate on both sides.

pairs.pair_note: Both pass; TRUMP is the sharper serve.

hints.reason: Bridge is the trump-based card game and diamonds are a suit that is named trumps, one card-table route.
Bridge is a card game and diamonds are a card suit, both immediate.
Bridge deck is a real structural term and bridge is played with a deck of cards; diamonds are one suit in that deck, a slightly less direct but still fair route.

best_available.why: Shortest path to both words with no stretch.

pairs.pair_note: All three pass via the card game; DECK is the weakest because diamond is reached only through the deck's contents.

hints.reason: The Rainbow Bridge is the widely shared pet-afterlife phrase for a dog that has died, a single familiar story reaching both words.

best_available.why: The Rainbow Bridge poem is well known among pet owners and unites both targets.

pairs.pair_note: No pass; CRACK is a one-and-a-half-sided hint.

best_available.why: Bridge over the river, fish in the river.

hints.reason: The bridge of a pair of glasses is a great route, but GLASSES is the plural of the target GLASS and contains it, a rule failure.
Spectacles have a bridge that sits on the nose, and spectacles are glass lenses / another word for glasses, reaching both legally.

best_available.why: Same eyewear route as GLASSES without containing the target.

pairs.pair_note: SPECTACLES is the legal version of GLASSES; slightly formal but widely understood.

hints.reason: Golden Gate Bridge is the obvious route, but GOLDEN contains and inflects the target GOLD, a rule failure.
GATE summons the Golden Gate Bridge, a familiar phrase that supplies both the bridge and, through 'Golden', the gold; fair in the way BROOKLYN is for APPLE+BRIDGE.

best_available.why: Legal route to the Golden Gate Bridge, which carries gold in its name.

pairs.pair_note: GATE is a two-step via one very famous name; GOLDEN fails only on the rule.

hints.reason: A violin has a bridge and its bow is strung with horsehair, a real single-object route, but both facts are musician's knowledge rather than common currency.
Bridge of the nose is direct, but a horse's nose is no more distinctive than any animal's, so the horse side is weak.
Wooden bridge is an ordinary compound and the wooden horse (Trojan horse, rocking horse) is famous, so the material route is specific on both sides.

best_available.why: Trojan/rocking horse plus wooden bridge are both instant.

pairs.pair_note: WOODEN carries the pair; VIOLIN is clever but niche, NOSE is half-generic.

hints.reason: Water freezes to ice, and the road sign 'Bridge Ices/Freezes Before Road' makes bridges freezing a familiar scene for drivers.

best_available.why: The bridge-freezes-first sign is well known and the ice side is trivial.

pairs.pair_note: Passes; bridge side is strongest for North American drivers.

hints.reason: Iron rusts by definition and a rusty old iron bridge is a familiar image, so one process reaches both.
Girder bridge and iron/steel girder are both standard engineering compounds, slightly technical vocabulary.
Riveted iron bridges are a classic image and rivets are iron/steel fasteners; the iron side is a made-of route but a vivid one.

best_available.why: Most everyday word of the three with a clear picture on both sides.

pairs.pair_note: Three passes in the same industrial scene; RIVET is the most niche.

hints.reason: Toll bridge is direct, but 'kings levied tolls' is a historical explanation invented to rescue the word; no player sees king from toll.

Beam bridge / bridge beams and light beam are both everyday compounds, an excellent double.

best_available.why: Compound on both sides with zero stretch.

pairs.pair_note: BEAM and RAINBOW both pass; TOWER's light side is loose.

hints.reason: Guardian lion statues are a strong image and stone lions do flank famous bridges, but statue alone does not clearly point at a bridge for most players.

hints.reason: Crescent moon is direct, but 'crescent bridge' is not a phrase; the bridge side is only that an arched span is crescent-shaped.
Bridge over (troubled water, a river) and 'over the moon' / the cow jumped over the moon are both stock phrases.
Arch bridge is direct, but the moon is reached only by shape (a crescent or the moon's arc across the sky), which is not a recognized phrase.

best_available.why: Idiomatic on both sides and instantly readable.

pairs.pair_note: OVER carries the pair; CRESCENT and ARCH both rely on shape for the weaker side.
